2028 Honda CR-V's New Mid-Size Platform Features Nearly 40% High-Strength Steel
10 photos
Photo: Honda
Japanese automaker Honda is rolling out a new vehicle platform, starting with the Avancier three-row SUV. To be used by the next CR-V, Accord, and Civic, this C- and D-segment architecture prides itself on controlled structural flex designed to manage tire loads while cornering, thus giving the suspension a better chance of doing its job while keeping curb weight under control.
The modular platform is described by its maker as having five sections connected by three fixed dimensions. With this arrangement, many Honda and Acura models can share large portions of the underlying structure while accommodating different vehicle heights, ground clearances, and driving positions.
An interesting part of its design is the New Handling Stability Rigidity Management system, which deliberately varies body stiffness in accordance with the loads individual areas must handle. While increasing panel thickness and strengthening joints may come as a sensible approach to improving rigidity, adding weight compromises tire behavior when cornering.
The second-largest Japanese automaker by global sales after Toyota argues that excessive stiffness can make it harder to manage how the tires behave when the suspension loads and unloads. Based on this information, engineers developed areas where controlled deformation smoothens load transfers.
Large project leader and Avancier chief engineer Hidenori Hamashima underlined that his team targeted nearly twice the vertical rigidity at the damper mounts compared to the previous-gen platform. They also used CAE to explore ways of controlling vibration through component stiffness instead of adding sound-deadening material everywhere. The rear brake caliper's relocation forms part of that effort.
Photo: Honda How come? As it happens, Honda moved the rear calipers from behind the rear axle toward the front, bringing them closer to the vehicle's center of rotation. This move reduces inertial inputs, limiting road noise without adding weight through sound-deadening measures. The body-in-white structure, on the other hand, is now made of nearly 40 percent high-tensile steel.
Said high-tensile steel is listed with 980 megapascals of tensile strength, a grade that is strong enough to prevent cabin intrusion during severe crashes while being ductile enough to be stamped into complex shapes without cracking. Because 980 MPa steel is stronger than conventional mild steel, thinner sheet gauges achieve similar structural load capacities.
For this platform, Honda established minimum thickness requirements for each structural member according to stiffness and NVH targets. The Japanese manufacturer also redesigned the front suspension, dropping the steel extension previously mounted ahead of the subframe. Aluminum front lower arms and knuckles are featured, reducing weight and road noise.
For the damper mounts, Honda decided on a crimped construction that increases rigidity without adding extra material. The connections between the knuckles and hub bearings have been stiffened, and suspension geometry was revised for improved lateral rigidity at tire contact points.
Photo: Honda
Then there's the electric power steering system, which receives a torsion bar with greater torsional rigidity for improved stability. Out back, the curved trailing arms have been replaced with straighter components. Honda further reshaped the lower arms with flatter undersides, all in the name of aero.
The rear lower arms now boast a double-plate and double-plate arrangement, reducing weight while allowing shorter arms to improve braking stability. As far as the engine compartment is concerned, Honda achieved a staggering 90 percent commonality across all of this platform's applications.
Shared parts include mounting brackets, wiring, and piping, with Honda claiming a 10-kilo (22 pounds) weight saving to boot. Honda standardized the high-voltage battery position beneath the second-row seats across both SUVs and sedans. The current CR-V and Accord hybrids carry them in the spare tire-pan area and under the rear seats, respectively.
Honda paid attention to the driver's relationship with the steering wheel and pedals as well. The company's so-called skeletal standard puts 140 millimeters (5.5 inches) between the footrest and the loud pedal, and the footrest angle moves close to the accelerator pedal's angle. Honda uses two distinct footrest angles to account for the different seating positions of SUVs and sedans.
The steering wheel angle, meanwhile, increases by one degree. Its telescopic adjustment range grows by 10 mils (0.4 inches). Together, both changes enable a more comfortable driving posture by allowing drivers to keep their arms more relaxed.
